chunks: "The impedance of a capacitor is Z C equals 1 over j omega C , where omega equals 2 pi f . You can also write it as - j over omega C , or in the Laplace domain as 1 over sC .
It comes straight from i equals C dv over dt .
If the voltage is a sinusoid, V e to the j omega t , taking the derivative just multiplies by j omega , so the current is j omega C times the voltage, and V over I equals 1 over (j omega C) .
Two things fall out of it.

The magnitude is 1 over (2 pi fC) , so it's inversely proportional to frequency and capacitance: at DC it's infinite, so a capacitor is an open circuit, and at high frequency it goes toward zero, so it looks like a short.
And the -j means the phase is minus 90°: the current leads the voltage by a quarter cycle. As a quick number, a 100 nanofarads capacitor at 1 megahertz is about 1.
6 ohms, and at 1 kilohertz it's about 1. 6 kilohms.
The one caveat is that a real capacitor has series inductance, so above its self-resonant frequency the impedance starts rising again instead of continuing to fall."
